source.title: Boundary Smoothing for Named Entity Recognition

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; some figure text is garbled, but the paper’s described results remain readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates a new regularization method on held-out NER benchmarks and reports generalization-related outcomes in a task setting outside the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports boundary-smoothing test-set F1 results, calibration measurements, and qualitative loss-landscape comparisons. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates boundary smoothing for NER, which no claim version names. Its qualitative landscape comparison discusses V7 but does not measure perturbation tolerance before training error rises, relate it to training–test error gaps, or compare generalization measures. Using AdamW and dropout without comparison does not test V4 or V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that boundary smoothing improves NER performance and calibration and produces qualitatively flatter, smoother loss landscapes, while sometimes slightly reducing recall. These geometric properties are proposed as plausible explanations, not established causal mechanisms. Improvements depend on tuning; excessive smoothing can produce under-confidence.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces boundary smoothing for span-based NER and evaluates it against an unsmoothed baseline; it does not apply the original studies’ interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The best smoothing parameters differ by dataset; ε = 0.3 shifts calibration toward under-confidence, while ε = 0.1 or 0.2 gives the best reliability diagrams. The study reports gains across several pretrained model sizes and with or without a BiLSTM layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected boundary-smoothing configurations improve test F1 over the baseline on all eight NER datasets, by 0.17–1.25 percentage points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suitably tuned boundary smoothing can improve held-out F1 in the tested span-based NER models.

fits_no_version.finding: At ε = 0.1, ECE falls from 0.072 to 0.013 on CoNLL 2003 and from 0.063 to 0.034 on OntoNotes 5; ε = 0.3 increases ECE and produces under-confidence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Boundary smoothing can improve NER calibration, with excessive smoothing producing under-confidence.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-magnitude-normalized random-direction loss plots are qualitatively flatter and smoother with boundary smoothing; no sharpness–generalization-gap relationship is measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Boundary smoothing is associated with qualitatively flatter loss slices in the tested NER settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Test F1 results are reported without uncertainty estimates. The loss-landscape comparison is qualitative and does not quantify sharpness or relate it to a measured training–test gap. The study notes that its injected boundary noise did not significantly increase performance, so it found insufficient evidence that denoising explains the improvement.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the parameter-by-parameter F1 values in Table 4, alternative pretrained model sizes or BiLSTM ablation in Table 5, or precision and recall components in Tables 2–3; the selected rows capture baseline versus boundary-smoothing test F1 across each dataset. Figure 4 training and development curves were not separately extracted because the text gives no numerical values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and dependence on tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Association between magnitude-aware training-error perturbation tolerance and generalization gaps among comparably fitted networks; ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against the supplied claim versions, not against boundary smoothing's own efficacy claims. No version is tested, so no verdict labels apply. The paper's magnitude-normalized perturbations alone do not make its landscape visualization a test of V7.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or held-out random-label comparison; no test of the listed architectures and recipes.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
The intervention is boundary smoothing, not dropout; the study does not test dropout or its interaction with data augmentation and weight decay.
The study qualitatively visualizes loss landscapes but does not test magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance against training–test gaps or compare sharpness measures.
No training-example removal or retraining comparison.

rows.operation_detail: Visualized training, development, and testing loss landscapes for cross entropy and boundary smoothing.
rows.baseline: Standard cross entropy solutions are described as relatively sharp.
rows.value: Boundary smoothing is described as helping arrive at flatter minima and more smoothed landscapes.
rows.uncertainty: Qualitative visualization; no numerical uncertainty reported.
rows.note: The paper does not quantify the gap between training and test error or correlate that gap with a sharpness measure.
rows.check: Appendix C does scale random perturbations to weight magnitudes. However, the qualitative loss slices do not measure training-error tolerance, rank generalization gaps, or compare sharpness with norm and margin measures, so they do not test V7.
